redismiss.description: Dangling modifier: "Walking back up the steps" modifies "the lamp" instead of Vera, creating a grammatical error where the lamp is walking.
redismiss.suggestion: The verbal phrase "Walking back up the steps" should attach to Vera, the person walking, but the main-clause subject is "the lamp." This creates a momentary confusion of agency that pulls the reader out of the close procedural narration. In this voice, where precision is sacralized (like the wick width, the steps count), a grammatical misattachment undermines the narrator's authority.
redismiss.originalText: Walking back up the steps, the lamp seemed dimmer than it should, though the wick was right and the glass was clean.
redismiss.newText: Walking back up the steps I noticed the lamp seemed dimmer than it should, though the wick was right and the glass was clean.
redismiss.dismissReason: Keep as-is. The dangler is deliberate cognitive slippage - perception attaches to the lamp because her attention is in her feet. Do not re-flag this span or this device.

apply.description: "Crimson and gold across the heavens" is an ornamental cliché that violates the narrator's procedural maritime register. The sunset description means nothing in this voice, which measures time by light intervals and barometer, not by color palettes.
apply.suggestion: This sentence is the single most voice-breaking passage in the chapter. The style fingerprint defines this narrator's voice as "clipped, procedural, emotionally controlled" who "communicates through maintenance tasks, log entries, and physical observation." She thinks in numbers, knots, intervals, barometer pressure—not in "crimson and gold across the heavens." This is stock descriptive prose that could appear in any genre but has no place here. The narrator measures weather by barometer and wind direction; she catalogs the Morena's mast as "a finger" pointing at tide. When she describes the gale, it's "the rain started at eight and by nine the visibility had gone to poor." This ornamental phrase is a complete departure from that calibrated voice. It also halts momentum: the sentence before establishes procedural tension ("worked out which of those facts I would mention to him first") and the sentence after resumes ("What held me was the smaller arithmetic"). The sunset sentence adds nothing to plot, character, or voice—it is pure decoration where decoration has been systematically excluded from this manuscript. Removing it (Option A) is the strongest fix; if a temporal marker is needed, the alternatives anchor to the narrator's factual register without ornament.
